verdicts.evidence: The if condition directly compares os.name, with os imported in the same function and no intervening rebinding (f1:12-13, s1).
The then arm follows the direct equality comparison os.name == "nt", without negation or an early exit reversing its polarity (s1, s2).
The condition reads the operating-system identifier os.name, so the os category fits (s1).
Both supplied versions have one if condition, c1, enclosing the indicated body; there are no additional conditions or alternatives, so the minimum is one (s2, s3, s4).
In the supplied derived code the condition enables the request and execution of its response; no else payload or environment-selected destination appears (f2:13-18, s4).
Equality with the Windows operating-system identifier enters the payload body, supporting activate; the condition does not test an analysis or sandbox property (s1, s4).

The operating-system check restricts the download-and-execute body to Windows while the ordinary install call follows outside it, supporting targeting rather than a choice of platform-specific implementations (s4, f2:18).

The original body is on the guard's then side, and the supplied derived version preserves that guard with both request and exec calls directly inside its body; no intermediate witness hops are needed (s2-s6).

The complete supplied files place the payload calls only inside run's os.name guard; registering the class as the install command does not bypass the condition, and no alternate payload caller appears (f1:10-38, f2:10-38).
The supplied derived code imports requests and uses its get method to retrieve response text, then passes that text through tag removal into the built-in exec call (f2:14-16, s5, s6).
